paras: The Marshville freight train shooting took place in Marshville, North Carolina, on Thursday, 28 July 1910, when Policeman Ashcraft chased and fired on two Black men who had jumped from a freight train. One of the men was thought to be the killer of a constable, but the man caught proved to be only a train rider, and the other escaped.
About a week earlier, according to the Monroe Journal, Constable Sing had been shot and killed at McFarlan by a Black man who had not been identified by name.

On the Thursday, two Black men jumped from a freight train at Marshville and "took to their heels," causing what the paper called "a great deal of excitement" in the town. It was "supposed" that one of them was the man wanted for Sing's death. Policeman Ashcraft pursued one of the men and fired three shots, and J. E. Bailey, hearing the shots, ran out and caught him. The other man was then chased and escaped after Ashcraft fired one shot at him.

The captured man turned out to be, in the Journal's words, "nothing more than just a stray fellow beating the train." No injury to either man is reported, and the coverage does not say what became of the captured man or whether the man who escaped was sought further.

The only known report appeared in the Monroe Journal of 2 August 1910 as the opening item of its Marshville column, under the headline "Excitement Over a Pair of Tramps." The item called both men "negroes" and ran beside notices of local deaths and remarks on late crops, offering no comment on the shots fired at a man who proved not to be the suspect. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press or in other white papers.

reader.title: Marshville freight train shooting
bases: A town policeman pursued and fired on two Black men who fled a freight train on suspicion that one had killed a constable; no mob or crowd is described (A1).
Only the Monroe Journal's Marshville column reports the episode, and no other paper in either press was found (A1).
